<p class="lx-eyebrow">The Plains market for one year: 3,000 MW of wind, 1,200 MW of solar, 700 MW of gas peakers (illustrative)</p>
<ol>
<li>On a spring midday wind and sun exceed demand and the price is −$25.00/MWh; on a summer evening only 401 MW are spare and scarcity pricing lifts it to $586.76.</li>
<li>Over the year the price averages $35.79/MWh, with 111 negative-price hours and 155 scarcity hours.</li>
<li>From 1,200 to 2,800 MW of solar, solar's capture price falls from $33.16 to $7.38 per MWh.</li>
<li>Energy-only, a new peaker falls $25 per kW a year short of its fixed cost; at 600 MW of peakers it pays, and the year has 2 hours short.</li>
<li>With a capacity market the capacity price is $191/MW-day, and consumers pay $40.79/MWh against $39.89 energy-only (table below).</li>
</ol>
<div class="a3-tables">

::: {#explain .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="a3-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Energy-only market</dt><dd>Plants earn only from selling energy; scarcity prices in a few hours pay for capacity that is rarely used.</dd>
<dt>Capacity market</dt><dd>A planner sets how much capacity to buy, and an auction pays for it on top of energy prices.</dd>
<dt>Reserve products</dt><dd>Spare capacity is priced hour by hour together with energy, in either kind of market.</dd>
<dt>Capture price</dt><dd>The average price a plant's output earns; for solar it falls as more solar sells in the same hours.</dd>
<dt>Missing money</dt><dd>The gap between what a needed plant earns from energy and what it costs to keep.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>What the toy leaves to real markets</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Scarcity curves are drawn by rules.** ERCOT priced reserves with an operating reserve demand curve from 2014; since 5 December 2025 it prices energy and reserves together.
- **Capacity demand curves.** Real auctions buy along a sloped curve, not a fixed amount, with caps and floors set in tariffs.
- **Accreditation moves money.** A capacity price is paid on rated MW, so the ratings of lesson <a href="a05-adequacy.html">A5</a> decide who earns it.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The clearing in symbols</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Price.** $p_t = c_{m(t)} + (\bar p - c_{m(t)})\,\max(0, 1 - s_t/600)^2$, where $c_{m(t)}$ is the last offer needed, $s_t$ the spare MW and $\bar p$ the cap.
- **Margin.** A plant earns $\sum_t (p_t - c)\,q_t$ a year; it pays if that, per kW, tops its fixed cost.
- **Capacity price.** $(F - \pi)/0.93$ per rated kW a year, where $F$ is a new peaker's fixed cost and $\pi$ its energy margin.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
:::

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="a3-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="negative" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A negative price means the market is broken.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It means the last offer needed would rather pay than stop: here wind and solar keep a $25 credit per MWh, in 111 hours of the year.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="average" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A solar farm earns about the average market price.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth, once solar is common. Here its capture price is 93% of the average at 1,200 MW and 32% at 2,800 MW; in CAISO in 2023 it was 38%.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="free" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “An energy-only market avoids paying for capacity.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It pays through scarcity prices instead: with 700 MW of peakers here, consumers pay $39.89/MWh energy-only and $40.79/MWh with a capacity market.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="cap" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A capacity auction clearing at its cap can mean thinner reserves without certain outages.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. PJM's 2028/29 auction cleared at its cap, 6,831 MW short of its requirement, measured against a 1-in-10 criterion.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="a3">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="adder" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">The last offer needed is $39.37/MWh, the cap $5,000 and 401 MW are spare against a 600 MW threshold. Roughly what is the price, with the lesson's curve?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">$39.37</li><li data-value="b">$5,000</li><li data-value="c">About $585</li><li data-value="d">About $1,690</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>39.37 + (5,000 − 39.37) × (1 − 401 ÷ 600)² = 39.37 + 4,960.63 × 0.110 ≈ $585 per MWh. Step 1 shows $586.76: its spare is 400.7 MW before rounding.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="mwday" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">A capacity price of $69.59 per kW a year is how much per MW-day?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">$69.59</li><li data-value="b">About $191</li><li data-value="c">$25,400</li><li data-value="d">$0.19</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>69.59 × 1,000 ÷ 365 = 190.66, about $191 per MW-day: kW to MW, a year to days.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
:::
